model_annotation: The graph illustrates the relationship between trajectory length and the parameter γ for three categories: unsuccessful, all, and successful trajectories, as derived from Monte Carlo (MC) methods. The x-axis, labeled γ, spans a linear scale from 0.86 to 1.00, with tick marks at intervals of 0.02. The y-axis, labeled "Trajectory length," ranges linearly from 10 to 22, with major gridlines at intervals of 2. The red dashed line with circular markers represents the "Unsuccessful" trajectories, starting at a trajectory length of approximately 17.1 when γ = 0.86 and increasing to about 21.4 at γ = 1.00, showing a consistent upward trend. The blue dashed line with circular markers represents the "All" trajectories, beginning at approximately 15.4 when γ = 0.86 and rising to about 19.2 at γ = 1.00, also exhibiting a steady increase. The green dashed line with circular markers corresponds to the "Successful" trajectories, starting at a trajectory length of roughly 10.6 when γ = 0.86 and increasing to approximately 15.1 at γ = 1.00, showing a gradual upward trend. Error bars are present on each data point, indicating variability in the measurements.

model_annotations.English: The plot illustrates the relationship between trajectory length and the parameter γ for three categories of search outcomes—unsuccessful, all, and successful—within the context of guided search strategies in non-serializable environments. The x-axis represents γ, ranging from 0.86 to 1.00, with tick marks at intervals of 0.02. The y-axis represents trajectory length, scaled linearly from 10 to 22. The red dashed line with circular markers, labeled "Unsuccessful," shows that trajectory length increases from approximately 17.0 at γ = 0.86 to about 21.5 at γ = 1.00. The blue dashed line with circular markers, labeled "All," starts at around 15.5 at γ = 0.86 and rises to approximately 19.2 at γ = 1.00. The green dashed line with circular markers, labeled "Successful," begins at about 10.5 at γ = 0.86 and increases to roughly 15.0 at γ = 1.00. Error bars are present for each data point, indicating variability in the measurements.
